t: Minimum Total Cost to Process All Elements
o: We hold k resources, consume nums[i] to process each element left to right, and whenever resources fall short we buy +k chunks whose prices are 1, 2, 3, .... Because chunk price grows by 1 each purchase, buying several chunks at once for a deficit costs a consecutive run of prices. Example 2 buys 2 chunks (cost 1+2) then 3 chunks (cost 3+4+5) totaling 15. Naively purchasing one chunk at a time can take up to ~1e9 iterations per element (k = 1, nums[i] = 1e9), so we need a closed form for batch purchases.
k: If a deficit d remains, the number of chunks needed is t = ceil(d / k), costing prices c+1 .. c+t, i.e., t*c + t*(t+1)/2.
Greedy is optimal: delaying purchases never helps because prices only increase over time, and overshooting is harmless since leftover resources carry forward.

a.i: Literally perform operations one at a time: while resources < nums[i], pay the next price and add k. This mirrors the problem statement exactly and is easy to verify against the examples, but its running time is proportional to the total number of purchases, which can reach ~1e14 in the worst case (tiny k, huge values), so it is mainly a correctness reference.
s: For each x: while have < x, add nextPrice to cost, add k to have, increment nextPrice.
Subtract x from have; return cost mod 1e9+7.
a.t: O(total purchases) time — up to ~1e14 in adversarial cases (k = 1, large values), so potentially too slow; O(1) space.

a.i: When a deficit appears, jump straight to the required count t = ceil((x - have) / k). The prices paid are the consecutive integers c+1 through c+t, whose sum is t*c + t(t+1)/2, where c is the number of purchases already made. Update c += t and have += t*k. This makes the algorithm O(n) regardless of magnitudes; only the modular accumulation needs care because c and t can be huge.
s: Set have = k, c = 0 (purchases so far), ans = 0.
For each x: if have < x, compute t = ceil((x-have)/k); add (c mod M)*(t mod M) + t*(t+1)/2 to ans mod M; then c += t, have += t*k.
Subtract x from have; return ans.
a.t: O(n) time — one constant-time batch computation per element; O(1) space.

w: Always present the closed-form version as the final answer; the simulation is only a stepping stone and TLEs when k is small relative to values. Correctness hinges on the greedy exchange argument: any schedule buys the same multiset of chunk counts in the same order, so batching at deficit points is optimal. Overflow pitfalls: t*k and t*(t+1) approach 1e18 — use 64-bit (or the modular inverse of 2, 500000004, in fixed-width languages); Python big ints are safe. Edge cases: k larger than every prefix need (answer 0), and deficits spanning multiple elements. Follow-up: what if chunk prices grew geometrically, or resources expired?
